card.adopted: none
card.heard: pick the project, who used it, problem, my responsibility
card.say: Good evening. I'd pick the AI trip planner at KKday, because I was the technical lead there. The users were travelers on our Android app. They wanted to book tours and activities at their destination. The problem was that planning took a lot of time. They had to work out the budget, search products one by one, and put the plan together by hand. My responsibility started with the technical plan. I designed the agent, connected it to our product and order data, and built the core backend. The chat gives no reliable amount, so the user types the amount on that confirm screen; the model never fills it in. The server binds that authorization to the payer, recipient, amount and expiry; chat or model text can suggest a payment but never authorizes one. If the model calls the payment tool again, that call maps to the same intent and client ID, so it can never create a second transfer.
card.then: Next, the team and the parts I didn't own.

more: I also set the retry limit for those backend checks myself, and I capped it at two retries so a slow upstream call couldn't stall the whole plan.
updates: My responsibility ended at the app team's own screens; they built the UI, and I agreed the response format with them: day cards, product cards and map points. I also wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan, so Day 1 shows first while the rest is still being made.

Before users saw a plan, our backend checked the response structure, the product IDs and the location limits, and if a check failed it retried with the exact error, falling back to a safe default after the retry limit.
The result was about 300,000 planning tasks a day, including first plans and changes. I don't have conversion numbers, so I can't say it made people book faster.
The main trade-off was latency against completeness: streaming Day 1 early meant the later days could still change, so the client had to handle partial plans gracefully.

updates: I also wrote the reconnect logic, so a dropped connection resumes from the last event instead of starting the plan again.

turns.question: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?

card.problem: Walk one change I personally made from a user action through the UI, data or network path
card.adopted: none
card.heard: pick one change you personally made, walk the path
card.say: The change I made myself was the SKU calculation on the product page. Before, every tap on a date, package or ticket type recalculated all the prices and stock on the main thread. So I flattened the configuration and built a price and stock index once. I moved the work to Dispatchers.Default and sent results out through StateFlow. Tap to finished screen went from about one second to 300 milliseconds.

updates: The index is rebuilt only when the product configuration changes, so a stale price can't be shown after an edit.

The index is keyed by the full combination of date, package and ticket type, so a tap that lands on a combination with no entry falls back to a recompute for that one case instead of showing an empty price.

The ViewModel holds the selected combination in StateFlow, and the screen collects it with repeatOnLifecycle so it only updates while visible; on rotation the ViewModel keeps the selection, so the price doesn't flash back to empty.
The configuration comes from the product API, and I parse it off the main thread on Dispatchers.IO, so a tap never waits for parsing.

The cached copy is only used until the fresh response arrives, and if the fresh configuration differs, the index is rebuilt and the selected combination is re-checked against it, so a price shown from the local copy can be corrected once the network data lands.

One thing I'd add is process death. If Android kills the app in the background, the ViewModel is gone. So I'd save the selected combination in SavedStateHandle and rebuild the index from the cached configuration on restore.

So I'd save the selected combination in SavedStateHandle. When the user comes back, the screen restores the same date, package and ticket type. Then it looks up the price in the index again, so the user sees their choice, not an empty page.

The one gap I'd close is the index rebuild itself. On a big product it takes a moment, so I'd build it in the background and swap it in when it's ready. Until then the old index keeps serving prices, so taps stay fast.
The rebuild runs on the main thread today, so on a large configuration it can still cause a short jank; I'd move it to a background dispatcher and swap the index atomically once it's ready.

I'd keep the index behind a single reference and swap it in one step, so a tap always reads either the old index or the new one, never a half-built one. And I'd cancel the rebuild if the screen is gone, so we don't waste work.

The last thing I'd check is the price shown after a swap. If the new index gives a different price for the same combination, the screen should update it, not keep the old one. And I'd log how long a rebuild takes, so we know if it's getting slow.

card.say: At that moment I write one row in the local database: the client transfer ID, the payer and payee, the amount as a Long in cents (80 dollars = 8000 cents), the status "pending", and a timestamp. I write it through the repository, so the UI still reads only from that one place. To make it durable before the network call, I do the insert in a transaction and wait for it to commit, then start the request. I use Room with WAL, so the commit is on disk, not just in memory. The request only fires after that insert returns, so a crash right after sending still leaves the intent on disk.
card.then: Next I'd cover the offline read path.

updates: The insert runs on Dispatchers.IO, and if the insert fails, I don't send at all, and the user sees a clear failure. The proof is a failure test: I kill the process right after the request leaves, then replay the same client ID, and the ledger must show one transfer.

The one gap I'd close is the local row itself. If the user reinstalls the app, the local client ID is gone, so the app can't ask about that transfer by ID anymore. I'd keep the intent on the server side too, so the history list still shows it as unknown until the server answers.
Storing the client ID server-side also means the server has to treat a repeated ID from a different device as the same intent, so I'd key it on account plus ID rather than ID alone.

The server also needs to reject a repeat of the same ID with different details, like a different amount, so the amount and payee must match the first request. I'd also keep that record longer than any client can stay offline, and log every replay that misses it.
